Course

One spec, many targets: the t27 compiler

A .t27 file is a spec with tests. The compiler t27c turns it into Zig, Rust, C, Verilog and more, and its pipeline stops at every stage to check itself. This course walks the 9 stages: reading the text, shape and refusals, names and types, the cost estimate, the same answer from every backend, the output file, seals, trust in the compiler and the machine word. Every widget runs the fn bodies of one of 18 specs of the compiler, compiled to WebAssembly.

Course 12, 27 lessons, a live widget and a t27 spec each: how a .t27 file becomes Zig, Rust, C, Verilog and WebAssembly. Reading the text, shape and refusals, types, the cost estimate, the same answer from every backend, the output file, seals, trust in the compiler and the machine word. Every answer comes from a compiled spec.

All lessons

  • Module 1 · Reading the text

    A compiler starts with bytes. Five tiny tests sort a byte into a letter, a digit or a gap, three scanners walk a line, and a number is refused before it can overflow.

    1. 01 A letter, a digit or a gap
    2. 02 Where a word stops
    3. 03 How big a number may be

  • Module 2 · Shape and refusals

    An expression is read through 11 nested levels, a rendered expression can lose the right side of an operator, and a refused line gets one of 7 numbered reasons.

    1. 04 Who binds tighter
    2. 05 An operator with nothing after it
    3. 06 Seven ways to refuse a line

  • Module 3 · Names, types and branches

    Before it knows any types a compiler sees a type as text: its width, whether it is a suffix, a tuple the Verilog backend takes, and an if/else that is a value.

    1. 07 What a type name means
    2. 08 A tuple for Verilog
    3. 09 An if that is a value

  • Module 4 · The cost estimate

    Before any wire is placed the compiler counts: the delay of a path and the clock it allows, the power of the resources, the length of a wire and the size of a clock tree.

    1. 10 How fast can it clock
    2. 11 What it will draw
    3. 12 Wires and clock trees

  • Module 5 · The same answer from every backend

    Each case pins one silent miscompile: a minus that lost its bracket, a shared value gone stale, and bytes, slices and strings in the Rust backend.

    1. 13 Minus before a bracket
    2. 14 A value gone stale
    3. 15 Bytes, slices and strings

  • Module 6 · The output file

    A compiler writes files, and a file may already be there: when it may overwrite, where the generated marker must sit, and committed output nobody regenerated.

    1. 16 May the compiler overwrite
    2. 17 The mark of a generated file
    3. 18 Committed output nobody regenerated

  • Module 7 · Seals

    A seal is a receipt for a spec and its tests: how a stranger checks its parts, what receipt an agent reads before reusing a spec, and what a killed run leaves on disk.

    1. 19 A seal checked by a stranger
    2. 20 The seal receipt
    3. 21 A run cut mid-seal

  • Module 8 · Trusting the compiler

    Three questions about the compiler itself: a table of 9 compilers and 10 filters, 7 builds of one commit that did not give one binary, and a rebuild by 3 routes.

    1. 22 The compiler sieve
    2. 23 Seven builds, one commit
    3. 24 Diverse double-compiling

  • Module 9 · Down to the machine

    The last stage: a line of text becomes one 32-bit word, the word holds fields in 3 shapes, and the file around the words has a header a loader checks in a fixed order.

    1. 25 Text to a machine word
    2. 26 Pack an instruction
    3. 27 The program file header
